KEY MESSAGE 1...Dry through most of the day today with rain chances 
increasing overnight towards the outer Cape and Nantucket.

Broad high pressure extending from the Maritimes to the Ohio Valley 
across the northeast remains overhead today, though with the two 
centers in the Maritimes and over the Ohio Valley, we find ourselves 
between them in a weaker spot. This weakened area of high pressure 
becomes more noticeable as the day goes on with increasing cloud 
cover from the SE to the NW and especially into tonight with rain 
chances increasing over the outer Cape and Nantucket. These are 
associated with low pressure continuing to deepen near the mid-
Atlantic/Carolina coast. A slight warming trend continues as highs 
approach the low 60s and upper 50s.

As low pressure well to our south continues to strengthen, the 
pressure gradient between it and the high pressure over southern New 
England will start to tighten, increasing NE winds heading into 
tonight. This will be especially noticeable over the Cape and 
Islands, where gusts to 30 mph are a possibility by daybreak 
Tuesday. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...Chances for rainfall towards coastal areas for much 
of the workweek due to an offshore nor'easter well to the south. 
Main impacts from this system will be marine-based: rough seas, 
beach erosion, and strong winds.

Confidence for the track and intensity for the nor'easter well to 
our south remains somewhat lower than normal at this point in the 
forecast. Latest guidance (with the exception of the AIGEFS) appears 
to have backtracked a bit on the more NW shift and instead takes the 
system slightly north and east instead. What hasn't changed much, 
though, is that among the ensembles, their members have continued to 
keep the low's center location south of the 40N/70W benchmark once 
it does track out to sea. Aside from this, the general trend this 
week is a drier, somewhat warmer pattern developing as a broad ridge 
of high pressure remains over much of the northeastern US and into 
Ontario. Temperatures continue to moderate through the week with 
highs generally in the 50s and 60s, with cool nights in the 30s and 
40s. The exception remains parts of SE MA where rain chances tick up 
once again towards Thursday.

The latest high-res guidance has shown some of the showers 
associated with the northern precipitation shield of this nor'easter 
making their way up to southeastern parts of New England, mainly the 
outer Cape and Islands. Compared to previous runs, the latest global 
deterministic guidance has seemed to back off on any rain making it 
to even Nantucket, for tonight. Given the return to more of a north 
and east track amongst a lot of the guidance later this week, higher 
QPF has shifted back more towards just the Cape and Islands. The NAM 
remains a bit of an exception, as it is a bit more bullish with this 
system and indicates a signal for greater rainfall totals around 
1.5" towards the outer Cape. It does, though, also take the north 
and east jaunt for this system later this week. Ensemble 
probabilities remain between 20 and 50 percent for totals reaching 
or exceeding 0.5" by Thursday evening, which remain focused over the 
Cape and Islands. For measurable precipitation, probabilities 
generally up to 30 percent exist over much of the coastal plain in 
SE MA. The GEFS is the exception as probabilities reach up to 70 
percent, though there is a very tight gradient between that and the 
50 percent mark in SE MA for this same timeframe. Dry air aloft 
along with a very tight moisture gradient that looks to be focused 
over SE MA would limit the spread of any rainfall across anywhere 
north or west of the I-95 corridor. Again, the highest probabilities 
remain focused on Cape Cod and the Islands for the second half of 
the week. Despite the uncertainty with precipitation associated with 
this system over southern New England, marine impacts continue to 
look more significant as it remains relatively stationary over the 
same area, churning over the same waters for what appears to be most 
of this week. This will lead to seas building up to 15 ft offshore 
of Nantucket.

Briefly mentioned in the previous Key Message, the pressure gradient 
between this nor'easter and the high pressure over the northeast US 
will tighten greatly, increasing NE winds over the waters and 
towards the Cape and Islands, RI, and the coastal plain in SE MA. 
These start to really build up tonight and Tuesday as the low 
pressure deepens and drifts very slightly north and eventually east 
(based on most of the latest guidance). Not much has changed amongst 
the guidance regarding the possibility of gale-force winds,
